name: Lissabata / Sou Iha
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Tauern, Odo D. 1929. Beitrag zur Kenntnis der Sprachen und Dialekte von Seran (Fortsetzung). Anthropos 24(5/6): 953-981; section 'Kurze Grammatik der Sprache von Lissabata. Sou Iha. Lautlehre' (pp. 962-981).
catalog_locator: p. 963 (printed of the archive.org scan of Anthropos 24(5/6)), 'Kurze Grammatik der Sprache von Lissabata. Sou Iha. Lautlehre', paragraph beginning 'Die Betonung der Worte'.
catalog_quote: Die Betonung der Worte erfolgt immer auf der vorletzten Silbe. Allfällige Ausnahmen sind in dem Wörterverzeichnis mit einem besonderen Akzent versehen worden, wie beispielsweise néuke, zurück. In den Fällen, in denen ein Wort apostrophiert wird, bleibt der Akzent stehen, so daß das Wort scheinbar auf der letzten Silbe betont wird. Dieser Fall tritt oft ein, wenn das Wörtchen -ne (es) an ein Wort angehängt wird. So findet man z. B. hanán' statt hanane. Diphthonge gibt es nicht: daher werden alle zusammenstoßenden Vokale getrennt gesprochen.

new_statements.translation: Words are always stressed on the penultimate syllable. Any exceptions have been given a special accent mark in the vocabulary, for example néuke 'back'. In cases where a word is apocopated (written with an apostrophe), the accent stays in place, so that the word appears to be stressed on the last syllable. This often happens when the little word -ne ('it') is attached to a word. Thus one finds e.g. hanán' instead of hanane. There are no diphthongs: all abutting vowels are pronounced separately.

After the b>h and l>n correspondence tables (hulane/hunu/hatu/aheni; nawa-i, nanite, tapene, wanu, nanane, nane) and the f~p note (lafune), the paragraph reads exactly as quoted: 'Die Betonung der Worte erfolgt immer auf der vorletzten Silbe. Allfällige Ausnahmen sind in dem Wörterverzeichnis mit einem besonderen Akzent versehen worden…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Regular penultimate word stress; a few lexical exceptions (e.g. antepenultimate néuke) are marked with an accent; enclitic -ne 'it' is counted (haná-ne), and when its final vowel is dropped the stress surfaces as final (hanán'). Vowel sequences are heterosyllabic (no diphthongs), so the penult count treats each vowel as a syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical exceptions marked by accent in the (unpublished) Woerterverzeichnis, e.g. néuke 'zurueck'; apparent final stress after apocope before/with enclitic -ne (hanán' < hanane).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('Betonung der Worte') from Tauern's own 1911-12 fieldwork on 'Sou Iha', the language of Lissabata; the enclitic -ne shifts stress (i.e. counts in the penult window). Old (1929) impressionistic description; no modern phonology of Lisabata states stress (Collins 1983, Erniati 2017 silent).
new_statements.identity_note: Tauern describes 'Sou Iha', 'die Sprache von Lissabata', spoken (1911-12) in Lissabata, Noniali, Niwelehu, Sukaradja and Lissabata baharu, i.e. the Lisabata-Nuniali language lisa1239 as a whole (Glottolog dialects lisa1240 Lisabata-Timur, nuni1252 Nuniali, suka1244 Sukaraja, kawa1278 Kawa); his forms (hulane, nanite, wanu with *l > n) match Collins's Lisabata dialect rather than Noniali. Not to be confused with the 'Makabala' grammar in the same instalment (pp. 953-962, 'in Wakolo bei Lissabata'), which is an Alune variety.

sources.note: p.963 (Lautlehre of the Lissabata grammar): stress always on the penultimate syllable; exceptions marked with an accent in the (never-printed) vocabulary, e.g. néuke 'back'; when a final vowel is apocopated the accent stays put so the word appears final-stressed, esp. with enclitic -ne: hanán' for hanane. No diphthongs (adjacent vowels are separate syllables).
